item.title: GitHub Copilot Code Review with MCP and Agent Skills Now GA
item.description: GitHub Copilot code review now supports agent skills and MCP servers in GA, bringing team standards and third-party context into every pull request review.
item.content:encoded:
GitHub Copilot code review has reached a major milestone with the general availability of agent skills and MCP (Model Context Protocol) server support, announced on July 29, 2026. These features transform Copilot code review from a static analysis tool into an extensible platform that understands your team’s coding standards, integrates with your existing toolchain, and delivers context-aware feedback on every pull request.

What’s New — Agent Skills and MCP Go GA

On July 29, 2026, GitHub announced that agent skills and MCP server support for Copilot code review are now generally available for all Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise users. This marks the culmination of a public preview that began on June 2, 2026, and represents GitHub’s most significant investment in code review intelligence to date.

The GA release brings three core capabilities to every Copilot-powered code review:

  • Agent skills allow teams to define custom instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot loads during code review. These skills live in .github/skills directories as SKILL.md files and can encode anything from coding style conventions to security checklists.
  • MCP server connections pull live context from third-party platforms — issue trackers, documentation systems, service catalogs, and monitoring dashboards — directly into the review process.
  • Attribution labels on skill and MCP-generated comments, so developers can see exactly which skill or MCP server produced each piece of feedback.

All MCP tool calls during code review are restricted to read-only operations, a deliberate security boundary that GitHub has maintained since the preview phase. The GitHub and Playwright MCP servers are enabled by default, giving teams immediate value without additional configuration.

Agent Skills Deep Dive — Bringing Team Standards into Every Review

Agent skills are the most transformative part of this release. Instead of Copilot code review applying generic best practices, teams can now encode their specific standards, conventions, and workflows into reusable skill definitions that Copilot loads automatically when reviewing relevant code.

How Agent Skills Work

An agent skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file and optional scripts and resources. The Agent Skills specification is an open standard used by multiple AI coding systems, including Copilot, Claude Code, and others. Skills can be defined at two levels:

  • Project skills stored in .github/skills/ (or .claude/skills/, .agents/skills/) — these apply to everyone working on the repository.
  • Personal skills stored in ~/.copilot/skills/ (or ~/.agents/skills/) — these apply only to the individual developer.

When Copilot code review processes a pull request, it scans the relevant skill directories and loads any skills whose triggers match the code being reviewed. The skill’s instructions become part of the review prompt, guiding Copilot to check for team-specific patterns, flag anti-patterns, and enforce conventions that generic AI models would not know about.

Real-World Use Cases for Agent Skills

Use Case Example Skill Impact
Coding standards Enforce team-specific naming conventions, import ordering, or file structure Consistent codebase without manual linting config
Security policies Check for hardcoded credentials, missing input validation, or unsafe API usage Catch security issues before they reach production
Architecture rules Verify that new code follows layered architecture, dependency injection patterns, or repository conventions Maintain architectural integrity as the codebase grows
Testing requirements Ensure every new function has corresponding unit tests, or that test coverage meets thresholds Enforce quality gates at review time
Documentation checks Flag missing JSDoc comments, incomplete README updates, or missing API documentation Keep documentation in sync with code changes

The Skill Ecosystem

The gh skill CLI command, available through the GitHub CLI, lets developers discover and install skills from GitHub repositories. Community collections have already emerged, including anthropics/skills and github/awesome-copilot, providing a growing library of pre-built skills that teams can adopt or customize.

Ecosystem tools are also maturing around skills management. Tools like APM (Agent Package Manager), AGENTS.lock for dependency locking, and skills-sync for keeping skills up to date across teams signal that agent skills are evolving into a full package management category for AI coding tools.

MCP Server Connections — Pulling Context from Third-Party Tools

MCP server support is the second pillar of this release. While agent skills bring team-specific knowledge into reviews, MCP servers bring live, external context from the tools your team already uses.

What MCP Brings to Code Review

When Copilot code review encounters a change that references an issue, a service endpoint, or a documented pattern, it can query the relevant MCP server for additional context. For example:

  • An issue tracker MCP can pull the full description, comments, and acceptance criteria for a referenced issue, allowing the review to verify that the implementation matches the requirements.
  • A documentation MCP can fetch the latest API documentation or coding guidelines, ensuring the review checks against the most current standards.
  • A service catalog MCP can validate that new service endpoints, configuration changes, or dependency updates follow the organization’s operational guidelines.

Default MCP Servers

GitHub ships with two MCP servers enabled by default:

  1. GitHub MCP — provides context about issues, pull requests, repositories, and code owners directly from the GitHub ecosystem.
  2. Playwright MCP — enables Copilot to verify UI changes by understanding browser automation and testing patterns.

Configuration and Management

MCP servers are configured at the repository level under Settings → Copilot → MCP servers. Authentication tokens are stored separately under Settings → Secrets and variables → Agents, keeping credentials secure and out of configuration files. Any existing MCP configurations that teams have set up for the Copilot cloud agent automatically apply to code review, eliminating duplicate setup work.

Security and Governance — Read-Only MCP and Enterprise Controls

GitHub made a deliberate architectural decision with this release: all MCP tool calls during code review are limited to read-only operations. This means MCP servers can provide context and data to the review, but they cannot create, update, or delete resources.

Why Read-Only Matters

The read-only constraint is critical for enterprise adoption. Code review is a sensitive gate in the development pipeline — it is the last line of defense before code reaches production. Allowing MCP servers to write data during review would introduce unacceptable risks:

  • An MCP server could accidentally create issues, modify documentation, or trigger workflows based on incomplete review context.
  • A compromised MCP server could use write access to exfiltrate data or tamper with external systems.
  • Audit trails become significantly harder to maintain when review-time actions can modify external systems.

By enforcing read-only access, GitHub ensures that MCP servers enhance the review without expanding the blast radius of any potential compromise.

Enterprise Governance Features

For Business and Enterprise customers, administrators can control review intensity at the repository level. The Low and Medium analysis tiers give admins granular control over how much compute and reasoning power is applied to each repository’s pull requests. This is configured per repository, allowing teams to match review depth to code complexity.

The Medium Analysis Tier — Matching Review Depth to Complexity

Alongside the agent skills and MCP GA, GitHub introduced the Medium analysis tier during the June 2026 public preview. This tier routes complex pull requests to higher-reasoning models for deeper analysis, while keeping the Low tier for straightforward changes that need fast, cost-efficient review.

When to Use Each Tier

Tier Best For Model Type Cost Profile
Low Simple bug fixes, dependency bumps, minor refactors Fast, lightweight model Minimal — ideal for high-volume repos
Medium Architecture changes, security-sensitive code, complex business logic Higher-reasoning model Higher — invest where it matters

The tier system lets teams optimize the cost-quality tradeoff. A repository of utility scripts might stay on Low tier for all reviews, while a repository handling payment processing or user authentication might default to Medium. Administrators set the tier per repository, and the setting is shared across Copilot code review and the cloud agent for consistency.

Getting Started — Configuration and Best Practices

Getting started with agent skills and MCP for Copilot code review requires minimal setup. Here is a practical guide for teams ready to adopt these features.

Step 1: Create Your First Agent Skill

Create a .github/skills/ directory in your repository and add a SKILL.md file:

# Code Style Skill

Review pull requests for adherence to the team's coding conventions.

## Instructions

1. Check that all new functions include TypeScript type annotations.
2. Verify that imports are organized: external libraries first, then internal modules, then styles.
3. Ensure error messages use the team's standard format: `[ComponentName] Description of the issue.`
4. Flag any console.log statements that should be removed before merge.

Step 2: Configure an MCP Server

Navigate to your repository’s Settings → Copilot → MCP servers and add a new server configuration. For example, to connect to a documentation MCP:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "docs": {
      "type": "url",
      "url": "https://mcp.internal.example.com/docs"
    }
  }
}

Store any required authentication tokens under Settings → Secrets and variables → Agents.

Step 3: Set the Analysis Tier

In the same repository settings, choose between Low and Medium analysis tiers. Start with Medium for repositories where code quality is critical, and use Low for high-volume, low-risk repositories.

Best Practices

  • Start small — Create one or two skills that address your team’s most common review feedback. Expand as the team gains confidence.
  • Use attribution — The new attribution labels on skill and MCP comments help developers understand where feedback comes from. Encourage your team to read these labels to build trust in the system.
  • Iterate on skills — Skills are not static. Review and update them as your team’s conventions evolve. The gh skill CLI makes it easy to distribute updates.
  • Leverage shared configuration — Since MCP configs for the cloud agent automatically apply to code review, set them up once and benefit everywhere.
  • Monitor and adjust tiers — Review the quality of feedback on Low vs. Medium tier reviews periodically. Adjust per-repository settings based on observed outcomes.

The Bigger Picture — GitHub’s Platform Play and the Agent Skills Ecosystem

The GA of agent skills and MCP in Copilot code review is more than a feature release — it is a strategic move that positions GitHub at the center of the AI-assisted development ecosystem.

Open Standards Leadership

The Agent Skills specification is an open standard, not a proprietary GitHub format. By making the specification available to other AI coding tools, GitHub is betting that interoperability will drive adoption faster than lock-in. Claude Code already supports the same skill format, and other tools are expected to follow. This creates a virtuous cycle: more tools supporting the standard means more skills being created, which makes the standard more valuable for everyone.

The Emerging Skills Ecosystem

The community response has been rapid. Within weeks of the public preview, ecosystem tools began appearing:

  • APM (Agent Package Manager) — A package manager for agent skills, similar to npm or pip, enabling versioned skill distribution.
  • AGENTS.lock — A lock file format for pinning skill versions across a team, ensuring consistent review behavior.
  • Mother MCP — A proxy server that aggregates multiple MCP endpoints behind a single interface, simplifying configuration.
  • skills-sync — A tool for keeping personal and project skills synchronized across developer machines.

This ecosystem growth mirrors the early days of package management in the JavaScript and Python ecosystems, suggesting that agent skills are following a well-understood adoption curve.

Competitive Positioning

GitHub’s move also positions Copilot code review against a growing field of AI code review tools. By offering an extensible platform rather than a fixed set of review rules, GitHub differentiates on flexibility. Teams are not limited to whatever review patterns GitHub ships — they can encode any standard, integrate any tool, and build any workflow they need.

Conclusion — What This Means for Development Teams

The GA of agent skills and MCP support marks a fundamental shift in what AI-powered code review can deliver. Copilot code review is no longer a static analysis tool that applies generic best practices — it is now a platform that understands your team’s specific standards, integrates with your existing toolchain, and adapts to your workflow.

For development teams, the implications are clear:

  • Consistency improves — Agent skills ensure that every review, regardless of who performs it, checks against the same team standards.
  • Context matters — MCP connections bring live data from issue trackers, documentation, and service catalogs into the review, reducing false positives and missed issues.
  • Security is built in — Read-only MCP and per-repository tier controls give enterprises the governance they need without sacrificing capability.
  • The ecosystem is growing — Open standards and community tools mean that the investment in agent skills today will compound over time as the ecosystem matures.

GitHub Copilot code review with agent skills and MCP is available now for all Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise users. Teams that invest in building their skill library and configuring MCP connections today will be well-positioned as the AI coding tools ecosystem continues to evolve.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are agent skills in GitHub Copilot code review?

Agent skills are customizable instruction sets stored as SKILL.md files in your repository’s .github/skills/ directory. They let you define team-specific coding standards, security policies, and review rules that Copilot automatically applies when reviewing pull requests. The Agent Skills specification is an open standard used by multiple AI coding tools.

How do MCP servers work with Copilot code review?

MCP servers provide live context from third-party tools during code review. When Copilot reviews a pull request, it can query MCP servers for information from issue trackers, documentation systems, service catalogs, and other platforms. All MCP tool calls are restricted to read-only operations for security.

Is there any additional cost for using agent skills or MCP in code review?

Agent skills and MCP support are included with all Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise subscriptions at no additional cost. The Medium analysis tier may use higher-reasoning models that consume more compute, but there is no separate billing line item — it is part of your existing Copilot subscription.

Can I use the same MCP configuration for both Copilot cloud agent and code review?

Yes. Any MCP servers you configure for the Copilot cloud agent automatically apply to code review. This shared configuration eliminates duplicate setup and ensures consistent behavior across both surfaces. You can also configure code-review-specific MCP servers if needed.

How do I get started with creating agent skills for my team?

Create a .github/skills/ directory in your repository, add a SKILL.md file with your team’s instructions, and commit it. Copilot code review will automatically load the skill when reviewing relevant pull requests. You can also use the gh skill CLI command to discover and install pre-built skills from community collections like github/awesome-copilot.

item.title: Patchwork AI Review 2026: Open-Source Framework for Automating Development Gruntwork
item.description: Patchwork AI is an open-source framework that automates development gruntwork — PR reviews, bug fixes, dependency upgrades, and security patches via composable patchflows.
item.content:encoded:
What Is Patchwork AI? — Overview and Core Philosophy

Patchwork AI is an open-source framework from Patched Codes (YC S24) designed to automate the repetitive, non-creative parts of software development — what the team calls “development gruntwork.” Unlike AI coding assistants that generate new code from scratch, Patchwork focuses on the post-code tasks that consume developer time: reviewing pull requests, fixing bugs, resolving issues, upgrading dependencies, and generating documentation. The framework is built around a composable architecture of Steps, Prompt Templates, and Patchflows that can be chained together to create automated workflows. Licensed under AGPL-3.0, Patchwork has accumulated 1,569 GitHub stars and 105 forks as of July 2026, with its PyPI package (patchwork-cli) at version 0.0.124.

The core philosophy behind Patchwork is that not every development task needs human creativity. By identifying and automating the gruntwork — the predictable, pattern-based tasks that follow established rules — teams can free up developers for higher-value work. This positions Patchwork in a distinct niche compared to interactive AI pair programming tools like Aider or full development environments like OpenHands.

Key Components: Steps, Prompt Templates, and Patchflows

Patchwork’s architecture is built on three composable layers that work together to create automated workflows.

Steps

Steps are the atomic building blocks of any Patchwork workflow. Each Step performs a single operation — reading a file, calling an LLM, applying a diff, or committing a change. Steps are defined in YAML configuration files and can be combined in any order. The framework ships with a library of pre-built Steps covering common operations like code analysis, patch generation, and git integration.

Prompt Templates

Prompt Templates are Jinja2-based templates that control how Patchwork interacts with LLMs. They define the system prompt, user prompt, and response parsing logic for each Step that requires LLM interaction. This separation of prompting from code means users can customize how the AI behaves without modifying the underlying Python code. Templates can reference repository context, file contents, and previous Step outputs, enabling sophisticated multi-step reasoning.

Patchflows

Patchflows are complete, ready-to-run workflows composed of Steps and Prompt Templates. They are the highest-level abstraction in Patchwork and represent end-to-end automation for specific tasks. Patchflows are defined in YAML and can be shared, forked, and customized. The framework ships with 10 built-in patchflows, and the community can create and distribute additional ones through the patchwork-configs repository.

Available Patchflows — What Can You Automate?

Patchwork ships with 10 built-in patchflows that cover the most common development gruntwork scenarios:

Patchflow Purpose Input Output
AutoFix Automatically fix code issues from linters or static analysis Linter output or issue description Patched code with PR
PRReview Review pull requests for bugs, style, and security PR diff Review comments
ResolveIssue Fix a GitHub issue automatically Issue description Code changes + PR
DependencyUpgrade Upgrade dependencies to latest versions Dependency file Updated dependencies + PR
GenerateDocstring Add docstrings to functions and classes Source code Updated code with docstrings
GenerateREADME Create or update README documentation Repository context README file
AddLicense Add license headers to source files Source code Updated files with headers
CreatePR Create a pull request from changes Branch with changes GitHub PR
CommitMessage Generate commit messages from diffs Git diff Commit message
CodeReview Inline code review for specific files File path Review comments

Each patchflow can be customized through configuration files, allowing teams to adapt the behavior to their specific coding standards, review criteria, and workflow preferences.

Installation and Setup — CLI, PyPI, and Self-Hosted Options

Patchwork is designed to be easy to install and run in any environment. The primary installation method is through PyPI:

pip install patchwork-cli

Once installed, you can run any patchflow with a single command:

patchwork AutoFix --config config.yml

The CLI supports configuration files in YAML format where you specify the LLM provider, model, input files, and patchflow-specific parameters. Patchwork can also be run as a library within Python scripts, making it suitable for integration into CI/CD pipelines and custom automation tools.

For teams that prefer not to install Python dependencies, Patchwork is available as a Docker image. The self-hosted nature of Patchwork means all data stays within your infrastructure — no code is sent to external servers except the LLM API calls you explicitly configure.

LLM Flexibility — OpenAI, Open-Source, and Local Models

One of Patchwork’s strongest features is its LLM-agnostic design. The framework supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, which means it works with:

  • OpenAI (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3, o4-mini)
  • Anthropic (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus) via API proxy
  • Groq (Llama 3, Mixtral) for fast, low-cost inference
  • Together AI for open-source model access
  • Hugging Face endpoints for custom or fine-tuned models
  • Local models via Ollama, vLLM, or llama.cpp

This flexibility is critical for organizations with data privacy requirements. A financial services company, for example, can run Patchwork with a local Llama 3 model on-premises, ensuring no proprietary code ever leaves their network. The trade-off is that smaller local models may produce lower-quality patches compared to GPT-4o or Claude 4, particularly for complex code understanding tasks.

Patchwork’s Prompt Templates can be tuned for different models, and the framework includes model-specific configuration presets that optimize prompts for each provider’s strengths.

Patchwork vs Competitors — Aider, OpenHands, PR-Agent, Plandex

To understand where Patchwork fits in the AI development tools landscape, let’s compare it with the main alternatives:

Feature Patchwork AI Aider OpenHands PR-Agent (Qodo) Plandex
GitHub Stars 1,569 47,834 82,673 12,316 15,554
Primary Use Batch gruntwork automation Interactive pair programming Full agentic dev environment PR review automation Large-project coding agent
Interaction Model Non-interactive (batch) Interactive (terminal) Interactive (web UI) CI-triggered (auto) Interactive (CLI)
Focus Area Post-code tasks (review, fix, docs) Code generation and editing Full development lifecycle Code review only Multi-file planning and coding
License AGPL-3.0 Apache 2.0 MIT Apache 2.0 (CLI) / Commercial MIT
Self-Hosted Yes (CLI + Docker) Yes (CLI) Yes (Docker) Yes (CLI) Yes (CLI)
LLM Support Any OpenAI-compatible Multiple providers Multiple providers Multiple providers Multiple providers
CI/CD Integration Native (CLI) Limited Full (sandbox) Native (GitHub Actions) Limited
Best For Automating repetitive dev tasks Real-time coding assistance Full dev environment automation Automated PR reviews Large refactoring projects

Key Differentiators

Patchwork vs Aider: Aider excels at interactive code generation and editing in the terminal. It’s designed for developers who want an AI pair programmer that can discuss and refine code in real time. Patchwork, by contrast, is non-interactive and batch-oriented — you configure it, run it, and get results. This makes Patchwork better suited for CI/CD pipelines and scheduled automation, while Aider is better for active development sessions.

Patchwork vs OpenHands: OpenHands is a much larger project (82,673 stars) that aims to be a complete AI software development platform with a sandboxed environment, web browsing, and code execution. Patchwork is more focused and lightweight — it doesn’t try to replace your development environment but rather augments it with specific automation capabilities.

Patchwork vs PR-Agent (Qodo): PR-Agent is the closest direct competitor, focusing specifically on PR review automation. It has strong GitHub/GitLab integration and a commercial tier from Qodo (formerly CodiumAI). Patchwork offers broader capabilities beyond PR review (dependency upgrades, doc generation, issue resolution) but has a smaller community and less mature GitHub integration.

Patchwork vs Plandex: Plandex focuses on planning and executing large-scale code changes across multiple files. It’s designed for refactoring and feature development. Patchwork’s strength is in the smaller, repetitive tasks that follow predictable patterns — the gruntwork that Plandex and Aider don’t specialize in.

The YC S24 Pivot — From Open-Source CLI to Enterprise Regulated Ops

One of the most interesting aspects of Patchwork’s story is the company behind it. Patched Codes was part of Y Combinator’s Summer 2024 batch, initially building Patchwork as an open-source developer tool. The project received significant attention on Hacker News — the Show HN post garnered 116 points and 24 comments, while the Launch HN (YC S24) received 67 points.

However, the company has since pivoted. Patched Codes now focuses on enterprise regulated operations — fraud detection, banking reconciliation, and compliance automation. The open-source Patchwork CLI remains available and is still maintained, but the company’s commercial efforts are directed at the Patched enterprise platform, which targets regulated industries.

This pivot is a pragmatic move. The open-source developer tools market is notoriously difficult to monetize, especially for a small team competing against well-funded projects like OpenHands (82,673 stars) and Aider (47,834 stars). By targeting regulated industries — where compliance, audit trails, and automation of repetitive verification tasks are high-value problems — Patched Codes found a more sustainable business model.

The implication for Patchwork users is mixed. On the positive side, the company is still alive and maintaining the open-source project. On the negative side, the core team’s attention is now divided between the open-source CLI and the enterprise Patched platform. Community contributions and third-party patchflows will be increasingly important for Patchwork’s long-term health.

Pricing and Licensing — AGPL Open Source vs Patched Enterprise

Patchwork follows a dual licensing model:

Open Source (AGPL-3.0): The Patchwork CLI, all built-in patchflows, and the core framework are licensed under AGPL-3.0. This is a strong copyleft license that requires any derivative work distributed to users to also be open-sourced under AGPL-3.0. For internal use within an organization — which covers most development automation scenarios — AGPL-3.0 imposes no restrictions. You can freely use Patchwork to automate your internal development workflows without any licensing concerns.

Patched Enterprise (Commercial): The Patched platform is a separate commercial product targeting regulated industries. Pricing is not publicly listed and is negotiated on a per-enterprise basis. The enterprise platform includes features not available in the open-source CLI: audit trails, compliance reporting, role-based access control, and dedicated support.

The AGPL-3.0 choice is strategic. It protects Patched Codes’ commercial interests by preventing competitors from building closed-source products on top of Patchwork, while still allowing broad adoption for internal use. This is the same strategy used by MongoDB (before its SSPL transition) and other open-source companies.

Real-World Use Cases and Community Reception

Use Cases

1. Automated PR Review in CI/CD: Teams integrate Patchwork’s PRReview patchflow into their GitHub Actions or GitLab CI pipeline. Every pull request automatically receives AI-generated review comments for code quality, security issues, and style violations. This catches problems before human reviewers invest time.

2. Dependency Upgrade Automation: The DependencyUpgrade patchflow scans dependency files (requirements.txt, package.json, go.mod, etc.), checks for newer versions, and automatically creates pull requests with the upgrades. This keeps dependencies current without manual effort.

3. Automated Bug Fixing: The ResolveIssue patchflow can be triggered when a new bug is filed. It reads the issue description, analyzes the relevant code, generates a fix, and creates a pull request — all without human intervention. For simple bugs, this can reduce resolution time from hours to minutes.

4. Documentation Maintenance: The GenerateDocstring and GenerateREADME patchflows help teams maintain documentation quality. Run on a schedule or as a pre-commit hook, they ensure that new functions and classes have appropriate documentation.

Community Reception

Patchwork’s community reception has been modest but positive. The Hacker News discussions highlighted appreciation for the focused approach — reviewers noted that many AI coding tools try to do too much, while Patchwork’s narrow focus on gruntwork is a refreshing alternative. The 116-point Show HN indicates genuine interest from the developer community.

However, the community is small. With 1,569 stars and 105 forks, Patchwork has a fraction of the mindshare of Aider or OpenHands. The PyPI package shows active development (version 0.0.124 as of July 2026), but the pace of new features has slowed since the company pivot. Community contributions are welcome but the documentation for creating custom patchflows could be more comprehensive.

Pros and Cons — Where Patchwork Shines and Where It Falls Short

Pros

  • Focused value proposition: Patchwork doesn’t try to be everything. It targets a specific niche — development gruntwork — and does it well.
  • Composable architecture: The Steps + Prompt Templates + Patchflows model is elegant and extensible. Advanced users can create custom workflows for their specific needs.
  • LLM agnostic: Support for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint means no vendor lock-in. Use the cheapest or most private option for each task.
  • Self-hosted and private: All code stays on your infrastructure. Only LLM API calls leave your network, and those can be directed to local models.
  • CI/CD native: The CLI-first design makes Patchwork easy to integrate into existing automation pipelines.
  • AGPL-3.0 for internal use: No licensing cost for internal development automation.

Cons

  • Small community: 1,569 stars and limited community-contributed patchflows means less ecosystem support than competitors.
  • Company pivot risk: Patched Codes’ focus on enterprise regulated operations means the open-source CLI may receive less attention over time.
  • Limited GitHub integration: Unlike PR-Agent, which has deep GitHub/GitLab integration, Patchwork requires more manual configuration for repository integration.
  • Steep learning curve for custom patchflows: Creating new patchflows requires understanding the YAML configuration system, Jinja2 templating, and the Step execution model.
  • No web UI: Everything is CLI-based. Teams that prefer visual interfaces may find Patchwork less accessible.
  • AGPL-3.0 concerns for distribution: If you build a product that incorporates Patchwork and distribute it externally, AGPL-3.0 requires you to open-source your entire product.

Verdict — Is Patchwork Right for Your Development Workflow?

Patchwork AI fills a genuine gap in the AI development tools landscape. While Aider, OpenHands, and Cursor compete on interactive code generation, Patchwork focuses on the boring but essential work that follows code creation — reviewing, fixing, documenting, and maintaining. For teams that want to automate their CI/CD pipeline with AI-powered PR reviews, dependency upgrades, and automated bug fixes, Patchwork is a solid choice.

The ideal Patchwork user is a development team that:

  • Has established CI/CD pipelines and wants to add AI automation
  • Values data privacy and wants self-hosted code analysis
  • Needs to automate repetitive development tasks at scale
  • Is comfortable with CLI tools and YAML configuration
  • Wants LLM flexibility without vendor lock-in

The less ideal user is a solo developer looking for an interactive coding assistant, a team that wants a full AI development environment, or an organization that needs deep GitHub/GitLab integration out of the box.

Patchwork’s long-term trajectory depends on community engagement. With the parent company focused on enterprise regulated operations, the open-source project’s future relies on contributors adopting and extending the framework. The architecture is sound, the niche is real, and the tool works today. Whether it builds enough momentum to thrive independently remains to be seen.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Patchwork AI free to use?

Yes, Patchwork AI is open-source under AGPL-3.0 and free to use for internal development automation. You only pay for LLM API calls if you use commercial providers like OpenAI or Anthropic. The Patched enterprise platform for regulated industries is a separate commercial product.

How does Patchwork compare to GitHub Copilot?

GitHub Copilot is an interactive code completion tool that suggests code as you type. Patchwork is a batch automation framework for post-code tasks like PR review, bug fixing, and dependency upgrades. They serve different purposes — Copilot helps you write code, Patchwork helps you manage it after it’s written.

Can I run Patchwork with a local LLM?

Yes. Patchwork supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, including local models served through Ollama, vLLM, or llama.cpp. This makes it suitable for air-gapped environments and organizations with strict data privacy requirements.

What programming languages does Patchwork support?

Patchwork is language-agnostic. It works with any programming language because it operates on text files and git repositories. The quality of results depends on the LLM’s understanding of the language, not on Patchwork itself. Languages with strong LLM support (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java) generally produce the best results.

Is Patchwork still actively maintained after the company pivot?

Yes, Patchwork is still maintained as of July 2026. The PyPI package shows ongoing updates (version 0.0.124), and the GitHub repository remains active. However, the pace of new feature development has slowed compared to the project’s first year, and the core team’s attention is now divided between the open-source CLI and the enterprise Patched platform.

item.description: Patchwork is an open-source Python framework that automates development gruntwork — PR reviews, bug fixes, doc generation, and dependency upgrades — using composable LLM-powered patchflows.
item.content:encoded:
What Is Patchwork? — An Open-Source Framework for Development Automation

Patchwork is an open-source Python framework by Patched Codes that automates the repetitive development tasks — known as “gruntwork” — that consume roughly 30% of a developer’s time according to a Tidelift survey. Instead of treating AI as an autonomous coding agent, Patchwork takes a workflow-first approach: it provides composable “patchflows” that combine atomic steps, LLM prompt templates, and orchestration logic into repeatable automation pipelines. With 1,570+ GitHub stars, 174 PyPI releases, and 11 built-in patchflows covering everything from automated PR reviews to vulnerability fixing, Patchwork positions itself as the CI/CD-native alternative to interactive AI coding tools like Aider and Claude Code.

What Problem Does Patchwork Solve?

The core insight behind Patchwork is simple but often overlooked in the AI coding tool space: developers spend a massive portion of their time on tasks that are repetitive, well-defined, and low-creativity. A Tidelift survey cited by the Patchwork founders found that approximately 30% of developer time goes to code maintenance — fixing security vulnerabilities, updating dependencies, writing documentation, reviewing pull requests, and generating unit tests. These are tasks with clear inputs and expected outputs, yet they remain largely manual in most engineering organizations.

Patchwork’s answer is not to build a better AI pair programmer, but to create a framework where these gruntwork tasks can be fully automated and plugged directly into CI/CD pipelines. The framework treats each automation workflow as a “patchflow” — a directed graph of steps that can include LLM calls, git operations, static analysis tools, API integrations, and shell commands. This explicit, deterministic structure is a deliberate philosophical choice: Patchwork’s creators argue that LLM agents struggle with open-ended planning, so they designed the framework to constrain LLM usage to well-scoped, predictable tasks within defined workflows.

How Does the Patchflow Abstraction Work?

Steps, Prompts, and Workflows

Patchwork’s architecture is built on three core abstractions:

  1. Steps — Atomic, reusable actions. Patchwork ships with 48+ built-in steps including CallLLM (send a prompt to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), CommitChanges (git commit and push), CreatePR (open a pull request), ScanSemgrep (run Semgrep SAST scanning), ScanDepscan (dependency vulnerability scanning), ReadIssues (fetch GitHub issues), SlackAgent (send Slack notifications), BrowserUse (browser automation), CallSQL (database queries), and CallShell (arbitrary shell commands).

  2. Prompt Templates — Reusable LLM prompt templates that define how the model should process inputs. These are version-controlled alongside the patchflow configuration, making prompt engineering a first-class part of the automation pipeline.

  3. Patchflows — Composable workflows that wire steps and prompt templates together with orchestration logic. Each patchflow is a YAML configuration file that defines the sequence of operations, input/output mappings, and error handling.

This modular design means that creating a new automation workflow is often as simple as composing existing steps with a custom prompt template. The Patchwork team describes this as a “Lego set” for development automation — developers can snap together pre-built blocks to create custom workflows without writing significant new code.

Key Differentiator: Explicit Workflows Over Autonomous Agents

The most important philosophical distinction in Patchwork’s design is its rejection of the “autonomous AI agent” paradigm. While tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Aider give LLMs significant autonomy to explore codebases, make plans, and execute multi-step changes, Patchwork takes the opposite approach: it constrains LLM usage to well-defined, predictable tasks within explicitly defined workflows.

This is not an accident. The Patchwork founders, who come from a DevSecOps background building security tooling pipelines, have seen firsthand that LLM agents struggle with open-ended planning and can produce unpredictable results. By limiting the LLM’s role to specific, scoped operations within a deterministic workflow, Patchwork achieves higher reliability and predictability — at the cost of flexibility.

For teams that value consistency and auditability over raw AI capability, this tradeoff is compelling. A Patchwork patchflow either succeeds or fails deterministically; it does not go off on tangents or produce surprising side effects.

What Built-in Patchflows Does Patchwork Offer?

Patchwork ships with 11 built-in patchflows out of the box, each targeting a specific gruntwork category:

Patchflow Purpose Key Steps
AutoFix Automated vulnerability remediation ScanSemgrep → CallLLM → CommitChanges → CreatePR
PRReview AI-powered code review ReadPR → CallLLM → CommentPR
GenerateDocstring Auto-generate docstrings for code ReadCode → CallLLM → CommitChanges
GenerateREADME Create README documentation ReadRepo → CallLLM → CommitChanges
DependencyUpgrade Automated dependency updates ScanDepscan → CallLLM → CommitChanges → CreatePR
ResolveIssue From bug report to pull request ReadIssues → CallLLM → EditCode → CommitChanges → CreatePR
GenerateUnitTests Auto-generate unit tests ReadCode → CallLLM → CommitChanges → CreatePR
GenerateDiagram Generate architecture diagrams ReadCode → CallLLM → CreateDiagram
GenerateCodeUsageExample Create usage examples ReadCode → CallLLM → CommitChanges
LogAnalysis Analyze application logs ReadLogs → CallLLM → GenerateReport
SonarFix Fix SonarQube-flagged issues ScanSonar → CallLLM → CommitChanges → CreatePR

AutoFix — Automated Vulnerability Remediation

AutoFix is arguably Patchwork’s flagship patchflow. It integrates with Semgrep, a popular static analysis tool, to automatically detect and fix security vulnerabilities. The workflow is straightforward: Semgrep scans the codebase for known vulnerability patterns, Patchwork feeds each finding to an LLM with context about the vulnerable code, the LLM generates a fix, and Patchwork commits the change and opens a pull request.

The results are impressive. According to Patched Codes’ published benchmarks, AutoFix resolves 82% of Semgrep-flagged vulnerabilities with GPT-4 and 68% with Llama 3.1 8B. This means teams can automatically fix the vast majority of SAST findings without human intervention, reserving manual review only for the most complex or ambiguous cases.

PRReview — AI-Powered Code Review Automation

PRReview automates the code review process by reading pull request diffs, analyzing them with an LLM, and posting review comments directly on the PR. Unlike human code review, which can take hours or days depending on reviewer availability, PRReview completes in minutes. It can catch common issues like logic errors, security anti-patterns, style violations, and missing edge cases.

The key advantage over human-only review is speed and consistency. PRReview never gets tired, never skips a PR because of other priorities, and applies the same standards to every review. However, it is best used as a first-pass reviewer that catches obvious issues before human review, rather than a complete replacement for human judgment.

ResolveIssue — From Bug Report to PR

ResolveIssue connects directly to GitHub Issues. When a new issue is filed, this patchflow reads the issue description, analyzes the relevant codebase, generates a fix, and opens a pull request — all without human intervention. This is particularly powerful for well-defined bug reports where the fix is straightforward, such as null pointer exceptions, off-by-one errors, or configuration issues.

DependencyUpgrade — Keeping Dependencies Secure

DependencyUpgrade uses ScanDepscan to identify outdated or vulnerable dependencies, then generates upgrade patches using an LLM. The LLM analyzes the breaking changes between versions and adjusts the code accordingly. This addresses one of the most tedious and high-risk maintenance tasks in modern software development — keeping hundreds of dependencies up to date without introducing regressions.

Architecture and Technical Deep Dive

The Step Library — 48+ Reusable Building Blocks

Patchwork’s step library is the foundation of its flexibility. Each step is a self-contained Python class with a defined input schema, execution logic, and output schema. The 48+ built-in steps cover:

  • LLM Operations: CallLLM (generic LLM call), CallLLMWithPrompt (with template), CallLLMWithContext (with codebase context)
  • Git Operations: CommitChanges, CreatePR, CloneRepo, CheckoutBranch, MergeBranch
  • Scanning Tools: ScanSemgrep, ScanDepscan, ScanSonar, ScanCodeQL
  • Issue Tracking: ReadIssues, CreateIssue, CommentIssue, UpdateIssue
  • Communication: SlackAgent, EmailAgent, ZohoAgent
  • Browser Automation: BrowserUse (web scraping and interaction)
  • Database: CallSQL (query databases)
  • Shell: CallShell (arbitrary command execution)
  • File Operations: ReadFile, WriteFile, EditFile, SearchFile

This library makes Patchwork unusually extensible. A team that wants to build a custom workflow — say, “scan for hardcoded secrets, rotate them via a vault API, and open a ticket” — can likely do it by composing existing steps without writing a single line of Python.

LLM Flexibility — Any OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint

Patchwork supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, giving teams complete freedom over which LLM they use. Supported providers include:

  • OpenAI (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini)
  • Google (Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Flash)
  • Groq (Llama 3, Mixtral — fast inference)
  • Together AI (open-source model hosting)
  • HuggingFace (community models)
  • Local models via llama.cpp, Ollama, or vLLM

This flexibility is critical for enterprise adoption. Teams can use cheap, fast models (like Llama 3.1 8B via Groq) for high-volume, low-complexity tasks like docstring generation, and reserve expensive frontier models (like GPT-4) for complex vulnerability fixes where accuracy matters most.

CLI and CI/CD Integration

Patchwork is designed as a CLI-first tool, not an IDE plugin. This makes it a natural fit for CI/CD pipelines. A typical integration looks like:

# Install Patchwork
pip install patchwork-cli[all]

# Run AutoFix on every push
patchwork AutoFix --pr

This can be added to any CI system — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI — as a step in the pipeline. The framework handles authentication, git operations, and PR creation automatically.

Performance Benchmarks and Real-World Results

AutoFix: 82% Resolution Rate with GPT-4

The most concrete benchmark available for Patchwork is the AutoFix patchflow’s performance on Semgrep-flagged vulnerabilities:

Model AutoFix Resolution Rate Cost per Fix (est.) Best For
GPT-4 82% ~$0.05-0.15 Complex vulnerabilities, production code
Llama 3.1 8B 68% ~$0.001-0.005 High-volume scanning, non-critical code
GPT-4o-mini ~75% (est.) ~$0.01-0.03 Balanced cost-performance

The 14 percentage point gap between GPT-4 and Llama 3.1 8B illustrates the cost-performance tradeoff. For a team scanning 1,000 Semgrep findings per week, using GPT-4 would fix ~820 automatically, while Llama 3.1 8B would fix ~680. The difference of 140 fixes might justify the higher cost for critical code, while the cheaper model is perfectly adequate for low-risk areas.

Developer Time Savings — The 30% Maintenance Problem

The Tidelift survey finding that developers spend 30% of their time on maintenance tasks is the economic foundation of Patchwork’s value proposition. For a team of 10 developers with an average loaded cost of $150,000/year, that 30% represents $450,000/year in labor spent on gruntwork. If Patchwork can automate even 50% of that — a conservative estimate given the 82% AutoFix rate — the savings exceed $200,000/year.

Beyond direct cost savings, there are qualitative benefits: reduced developer burnout from repetitive tasks, faster security fix turnaround (from days to minutes), and more time for creative, high-value work.

Patchwork vs The Competition

The AI coding tool landscape has exploded since 2024, with dozens of tools competing for developer attention. Here is how Patchwork compares to the major alternatives:

Feature Patchwork Aider Plandex Continue Claude Code
Paradigm Workflow automation Interactive pair programming Plan-first agent IDE assistant Agentic coding
Interface CLI / CI/CD Terminal (interactive) CLI (interactive) VS Code / JetBrains CLI / Terminal
Primary Use Batch automation Real-time coding Complex multi-file changes Inline assistance Open-ended coding
LLM Autonomy Low (constrained) Medium High Medium High
CI/CD Native Yes No No No No
Stars (July 2026) 1,570+ 47,464+ 15,532+ 34,938+ N/A (proprietary)
License AGPL-3.0 Apache-2.0 AGPL-3.0 Apache-2.0 Proprietary
Language Python Python Go TypeScript TypeScript
Self-Hostable Yes Yes Yes Yes No

Patchwork vs Aider — Batch Automation vs Interactive Pair Programming

Aider is the most popular AI coding CLI tool with 47,464+ stars, and it represents the opposite end of the spectrum from Patchwork. Aider is designed for interactive pair programming: you sit in your terminal, describe changes, and Aider edits your code in real time with your approval. It excels at open-ended coding tasks where the developer wants to collaborate with AI.

Patchwork, by contrast, is designed to run without human supervision. You configure a patchflow, add it to your CI pipeline, and it runs automatically on every push or on a schedule. Aider is a tool for making changes; Patchwork is a tool for automating the process of making routine changes.

Choose Aider when: You need real-time coding assistance, complex refactoring, or exploratory development. Choose Patchwork when: You want to automate repetitive, well-defined tasks in your CI/CD pipeline.

Patchwork vs Plandex — Workflow-First vs Plan-First

Plandex (15,532+ stars) takes a “plan-first” approach: it analyzes a task, creates a plan, presents it to the developer for approval, and then executes the plan across multiple files. It is designed for complex, multi-file changes where planning is essential.

Patchwork’s workflow-first approach is more rigid but more reliable. A patchflow does exactly what it is configured to do, every time. Plandex’s plan-first approach is more flexible but introduces variability — the plan quality depends on the LLM’s reasoning, and different runs may produce different plans.

Choose Plandex when: You need to make complex, multi-file changes that require planning and human approval. Choose Patchwork when: You need deterministic, repeatable automation for well-defined tasks.

Patchwork vs Continue — CI/CD Tool vs IDE Assistant

Continue (34,938+ stars) is primarily an IDE extension for VS Code and JetBrains, providing inline code completion, chat-based assistance, and tab autocomplete. It is designed to augment the developer’s workflow within their editor.

Patchwork and Continue are largely complementary rather than competitive. A developer might use Continue for real-time assistance while coding, and Patchwork for automated PR reviews and vulnerability fixes in CI/CD. The overlap is minimal because they target different parts of the development lifecycle.

Choose Continue when: You want AI assistance inside your IDE for real-time coding. Choose Patchwork when: You want automated gruntwork in your CI/CD pipeline.

Patchwork vs Claude Code / Codex CLI — The Agentic Coding Landscape

Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex CLI (OpenAI) represent the newest category of AI coding tools: agentic coding assistants that can explore codebases, make plans, and execute multi-step changes autonomously. These tools give LLMs significant freedom to decide what to do and how to do it.

Patchwork’s constrained, workflow-first approach is philosophically opposed to this agentic paradigm. The Patchwork team explicitly states that “LLM agents struggle with planning” and designs around this limitation. For teams that share this skepticism about autonomous AI agents, Patchwork’s deterministic workflows are more trustworthy.

Choose Claude Code / Codex CLI when: You trust LLMs to plan and execute complex tasks autonomously. Choose Patchwork when: You want predictable, auditable automation with clear success/failure states.

Getting Started with Patchwork

Installation and Configuration

Patchwork requires Python 3.9+ and is installed via pip:

pip install patchwork-cli[all]

The [all] extra installs all optional dependencies including Semgrep, Depscan, and browser automation tools. For a minimal installation, use pip install patchwork-cli and install only the steps you need.

Configuration is done through a YAML config file or environment variables. At minimum, you need to set your LLM API key:

export OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here
# Or for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint:
export PATCHWORK_LLM_API_KEY=your-key
export PATCHWORK_LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.groq.com/openai/v1

Running Your First Patchflow

Once installed, running a patchflow is a single command:

# Generate docstrings for all Python files in the current directory
patchwork GenerateDocstring

# Run AutoFix with Semgrep scanning
patchwork AutoFix --pr

# Analyze application logs
patchwork LogAnalysis --log-file /var/log/app.log

The --pr flag tells Patchwork to create a pull request with the changes. Without it, changes are committed directly to the current branch.

Creating Custom Patchflows

Custom patchflows are defined as YAML files in a .patchwork/configs/ directory. Here is a minimal example:

# .patchwork/configs/MyCustomFlow.yml
name: MyCustomFlow
steps:
  - name: scan
    step: ScanSemgrep
    inputs:
      path: .
  - name: fix
    step: CallLLM
    inputs:
      prompt_template: |
        Fix the following security vulnerability:
        {{ scan.output }}
      model: gpt-4
  - name: commit
    step: CommitChanges
    inputs:
      message: "Auto-fix: {{ scan.finding_id }}"

This composability is Patchwork’s superpower. Teams can build a library of custom patchflows tailored to their specific stack, coding standards, and compliance requirements.

Enterprise Considerations

Self-Hosting and Data Privacy

One of Patchwork’s strongest enterprise selling points is that it is fully self-hosted. Unlike cloud-only AI coding tools, Patchwork runs entirely on your infrastructure. Code never leaves your network, LLM calls go to your configured endpoint (which can be a local model via Ollama or vLLM), and all git operations happen within your repository.

For organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements — financial services, healthcare, government, defense — this is a decisive advantage. No third party ever sees your source code, PR diffs, or vulnerability scan results.

AGPL-3.0 Licensing and Commercial Use

Patchwork is licensed under AGPL-3.0, with the patchwork-configs (custom patchflow configurations) under Apache-2.0. The AGPL-3.0 license has implications for commercial use: if you modify Patchwork’s core code and deploy it as a network service, you must release your modifications under AGPL-3.0.

However, for most use cases — running Patchwork as-is in your CI/CD pipeline, creating custom patchflow configurations, or integrating it with your tools — the AGPL-3.0 license does not impose additional obligations. The Apache-2.0 license on patchwork-configs means your custom workflows remain your own intellectual property.

Community and Support

Patchwork has 5 core contributors (CTY-git, whoisarpit, codelion, prathamjagga, patched-admin) and 194 open issues on GitHub, indicating active community engagement. The project has a GitHub community health score of 75% with a code of conduct, contributing guidelines, and issue templates.

Support is primarily community-driven through GitHub issues and discussions. As an open-source project without a commercial backing (beyond Patched Codes itself), there is no dedicated enterprise support tier. Teams that need guaranteed response times should factor this into their evaluation.

2026 Project Health and Roadmap

Development Activity and Community Growth

As of July 2026, Patchwork has 1,570+ GitHub stars and 104 forks — respectable but modest compared to Aider (47,464+) or Continue (34,938+). The project has 174 PyPI releases with the latest being v0.0.124 (April 2025), suggesting a mature release cadence.

Recent development activity includes LiteLLM integration for multi-provider AI gateway support, which simplifies enterprise deployments by providing a unified API across different LLM providers. The project’s 194 open issues suggest both active community engagement and a backlog of feature requests and bug fixes.

Roadmap Progress — Embeddings, Parallelization, Fine-Tuned Models

The Patchwork team has indicated several roadmap priorities:

  • Embeddings-based code understanding: Improving Patchwork’s ability to understand codebase context by using embeddings for semantic code search, which would improve the quality of LLM-generated fixes.
  • Parallel step execution: Running independent steps concurrently to reduce patchflow execution time, critical for CI/CD pipelines where speed matters.
  • Fine-tuned models: Developing specialized models for specific patchflow tasks (e.g., a model fine-tuned specifically for vulnerability fixing), which could improve accuracy while reducing cost.

These roadmap items suggest the project is evolving toward more sophisticated code understanding and better performance, while maintaining its core philosophy of explicit, deterministic workflows.

Verdict — Who Should Use Patchwork?

Ideal Use Cases and Team Profiles

Patchwork is best suited for:

  1. DevSecOps teams that want to automate security vulnerability remediation in CI/CD pipelines. The AutoFix patchflow with Semgrep integration is the most mature and well-documented use case.

  2. Engineering teams with high PR volume who need automated first-pass code review. PRReview can catch common issues before human reviewers invest time.

  3. Organizations with data privacy requirements that cannot use cloud-only AI coding tools. Patchwork’s self-hosted architecture with local LLM support is a strong fit.

  4. Teams practicing “shift-left” security who want to catch and fix vulnerabilities before they reach production. AutoFix in CI/CD catches issues on every commit.

  5. Open-source maintainers who need to automate documentation, changelog generation, and dependency updates across multiple repositories.

Limitations and Gaps

Patchwork is not the right tool for:

  • Open-ended coding tasks — If you need AI to help design architecture, implement complex features, or refactor large codebases, interactive tools like Aider or Claude Code are better choices.
  • Teams that want an AI pair programmer — Patchwork is automation, not collaboration. It runs without human input.
  • Small projects with minimal gruntwork — The setup overhead may not be justified for a solo developer or a small project with few maintenance tasks.
  • Teams that distrust LLM-generated code — Even with 82% AutoFix accuracy, 18% of fixes will be incorrect or incomplete, requiring human review.

Final Recommendation

Patchwork fills a genuine gap in the AI coding tool ecosystem. While most tools compete to build the smartest autonomous agent, Patchwork takes the less glamorous but arguably more practical approach of automating the boring, repetitive tasks that drain developer productivity. Its explicit workflow model, comprehensive step library, and CI/CD-native design make it a valuable addition to any engineering team’s automation toolkit.

For teams already using Semgrep, SonarQube, or similar static analysis tools, Patchwork’s AutoFix and SonarFix patchflows alone can deliver immediate ROI by automating the most tedious part of vulnerability management. The ability to run entirely self-hosted with any LLM backend makes it an attractive option for security-conscious organizations.

Patchwork is not a replacement for interactive AI coding tools — it is a complement. Use Aider or Claude Code for the creative, exploratory parts of development, and Patchwork for the gruntwork. Together, they cover the full spectrum of AI-assisted software development.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Patchwork and how does it differ from other AI coding tools?

Patchwork is an open-source Python framework that automates development gruntwork through composable, LLM-powered workflows called “patchflows.” Unlike interactive tools like Aider or Claude Code that act as AI pair programmers, Patchwork is designed for unattended batch automation in CI/CD pipelines. It constrains LLM usage to well-defined, predictable tasks within explicitly defined workflows, prioritizing reliability and auditability over flexibility.

Can Patchwork work with local LLMs for data privacy?

Yes. Patchwork supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, including local models running via Ollama, llama.cpp, or vLLM. This makes it fully self-hostable — code never leaves your network, and LLM calls can be directed to on-premise models. This is a key advantage for organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements in financial services, healthcare, and government sectors.

How accurate is Patchwork’s AutoFix for security vulnerabilities?

According to published benchmarks, AutoFix resolves 82% of Semgrep-flagged vulnerabilities with GPT-4 and 68% with Llama 3.1 8B. The 14 percentage point gap illustrates the cost-performance tradeoff: GPT-4 is more accurate but more expensive, while Llama 3.1 8B is cheaper and faster but misses more complex vulnerabilities. For most teams, a tiered approach using cheap models for high-volume scanning and expensive models for critical findings is optimal.

Is Patchwork free to use for commercial projects?

Patchwork is open-source under AGPL-3.0, with patchwork-configs (custom workflow configurations) under Apache-2.0. Running Patchwork as-is in your CI/CD pipeline or creating custom patchflow configurations does not require releasing your code. However, if you modify Patchwork’s core Python code and deploy it as a network service, AGPL-3.0 requires releasing those modifications. Most commercial use cases fall under the standard open-source usage terms without additional obligations.

What are the system requirements for running Patchwork?

Patchwork requires Python 3.9 or later and is installed via pip install patchwork-cli[all]. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows (via WSL). For LLM access, you need an API key for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — OpenAI, Google Gemini, Groq, Together AI, HuggingFace, or a local model server. Disk and memory requirements depend on the patchflow: simple workflows like GenerateDocstring need minimal resources, while AutoFix with Semgrep scanning may need several gigabytes for dependency databases.

item.title: VibeScaffold Review 2026: Turn Ideas into AI Coding Agent-Ready Specs
item.description: VibeScaffold generates AI coding agent-ready specs from plain ideas. Read our 2026 review covering features, pricing, competitors, and whether it delivers.
item.content:encoded:
VibeScaffold is a free, browser-based tool that turns a rough product idea into four structured specification documents designed to be fed directly into AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Instead of jumping straight to code and hoping for the best, VibeScaffold guides you through a wizard that asks the right questions upfront, producing ONE_PAGER.md, DEV_SPEC.md, PROMPT_PLAN.md, and AGENTS.md files that keep your AI agents aligned and productive from the first prompt to the final commit.

What Is VibeScaffold? — Overview of the Tool and Its 4-Document Output Format

VibeScaffold, created by product leader and fractional CTO Ben Shoemaker, launched on Hacker News in November 2025 and received 71 points with 37 comments. The tool addresses a growing pain point in the AI-assisted development world: AI coding agents are powerful, but they lack context. Without a shared specification, different agents working on the same project can contradict each other, lose track of requirements, or generate code that works in isolation but fails as a system.

The core output of VibeScaffold is a set of four markdown documents:

  • ONE_PAGER.md — A high-level project summary that captures the vision, target audience, core problem, and key features in a single page. This document is designed for stakeholders and serves as the north star for the entire project.
  • DEV_SPEC.md — A detailed technical specification covering architecture, data models, API endpoints, component trees, and implementation notes. This is the document developers and AI agents reference during implementation.
  • PROMPT_PLAN.md — A structured sequence of prompts designed to be fed into AI coding agents in order. Each prompt builds on the previous one, ensuring agents work through the project systematically rather than jumping around.
  • AGENTS.md — A project-level context file that AI coding tools read automatically. This file tells agents about the project structure, coding conventions, dependencies, and architectural decisions so they don’t need to rediscover them on every session.

The tool is entirely free to use with no signup required. The creator covers the inference costs personally, which is a deliberate choice to build adoption and gather feedback from the community.

The 80% Problem — Why AI Coding Projects Stall and How Specs Help

Anyone who has used AI coding agents extensively knows the pattern: the first prompt produces impressive results, the second prompt builds on that momentum, and by the tenth prompt you have something that looks like a working application. Then you hit the wall. The AI starts breaking things it previously built correctly. It forgets architectural decisions. It introduces inconsistencies that compound into bugs that are harder to fix than if you had written the code yourself.

This is the 80% problem. AI coding tools can get you 80% of the way to a working product with remarkable speed. But the final 20% — edge cases, error handling, cross-cutting concerns, performance optimization, and system integration — becomes exponentially harder without a shared specification that grounds every agent in the same reality.

The root cause is simple: AI coding agents have no persistent memory between sessions. Each new prompt is a fresh conversation. Even with context windows of 200K tokens or more, agents don’t remember what they decided three prompts ago unless that decision is captured in a document they can reference. Without specs, every agent is effectively building its own version of the project.

VibeScaffold solves this by making the specification the primary artifact. Instead of the code being the source of truth (which changes constantly and is hard for an LLM to reason about holistically), the spec becomes the source of truth. Code is generated from the spec, and when something breaks, you check the spec, not the code.

How VibeScaffold Works — Step-by-Step Walkthrough of the Wizard Flow

VibeScaffold uses a guided wizard format that asks progressively more detailed questions about your project. The flow is designed to be accessible to non-technical users while producing output that technical teams and AI agents can act on immediately.

Step 1: Project Overview — You describe your idea in plain language. What are you building? Who is it for? What problem does it solve? The wizard asks these questions in natural language, so you don’t need to know technical jargon to get started.

Step 2: Feature Definition — The wizard prompts you to list the core features of your application. It suggests categories based on your project overview and asks you to prioritize them. This step forces you to think about scope before you start building, which is one of the most common failure points in AI-assisted development.

Step 3: Technical Decisions — Based on your feature list, VibeScaffold asks about technical preferences: frontend framework, backend language, database, hosting, authentication approach, and API design patterns. If you don’t know the answer, it provides sensible defaults based on your project type.

Step 4: Agent Configuration — This is where VibeScaffold differentiates itself. It asks which AI coding tools you plan to use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, Aider, or others) and generates tool-specific configuration files that each agent can read. This ensures that Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex all share the same understanding of your project.

Step 5: Document Generation — VibeScaffold generates all four documents and presents them in a clean interface where you can review, edit, and download each one. The documents are linked to each other, so changes in one propagate to the others.

The entire process takes 10-15 minutes for a first-time user and about 5 minutes once you’re familiar with the flow. That is a small investment compared to the hours of debugging and rework that result from starting without a spec.

The Four Documents — ONE_PAGER.md, DEV_SPEC.md, PROMPT_PLAN.md, and AGENTS.md Explained

ONE_PAGER.md

The one-pager is the executive summary of your project. It covers the elevator pitch, target audience, core problem, key features, success metrics, and timeline. This document is designed for stakeholders who need to understand the project at a high level without diving into technical details. It also serves as the anchor document that the other three documents reference.

DEV_SPEC.md

The development specification is the most technically detailed document. It includes:

  • Architecture overview — System diagram description, component relationships, and data flow
  • Data models — Entity definitions, field types, relationships, and validation rules
  • API specifications — Endpoints, request/response formats, authentication, and error handling
  • Component tree — Frontend component hierarchy with props, state, and side effects
  • Implementation notes — Edge cases, performance considerations, and known trade-offs

This document is what you hand to an AI coding agent when you want it to implement a specific feature correctly the first time.

PROMPT_PLAN.md

The prompt plan is a sequence of carefully ordered prompts designed to be fed into AI coding agents one at a time. Each prompt builds on the output of the previous one. The ordering is intentional: foundational pieces (data models, database schema) come first, then business logic, then UI, then integration, then polish.

This is the document that makes VibeScaffold more than just a spec generator. It operationalizes the spec into an executable plan that an AI agent can follow without human intervention at every step.

AGENTS.md

The AGENTS.md file is a project-level context file that AI coding tools read automatically when they start a session. It tells the agent about:

  • Project structure and directory layout
  • Coding conventions and style preferences
  • Key dependencies and their versions
  • Architectural decisions and their rationale
  • Testing strategy and quality standards
  • Environment setup and configuration

This file is inspired by the CLAUDE.md convention that Anthropic introduced for Claude Code, but generalized to work across multiple AI coding tools. When placed in the project root, tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex read it automatically and adjust their behavior accordingly.

VibeScaffold vs. Competitors — Comparison with Spec-Driven-Development, Specdd, and Devplan

VibeScaffold is not the only tool in the spec-driven development space. Here is how it compares to the main alternatives:

Feature VibeScaffold Spec-Driven-Development (SDD) Specdd Devplan
Format Web wizard Claude skill Agent skill SaaS platform

The “Shift Left” Trend — Why Specs Matter More Than Code in the AI Era

Ben Shoemaker’s blog post on the “shift left” trend in AI coding argues that specifications are becoming more important than code in the AI-assisted development workflow. The logic is straightforward: if AI can write code faster and cheaper than humans, then the bottleneck shifts from code production to code specification. The quality of the output is bounded by the quality of the input.

This represents a fundamental inversion of the traditional software development hierarchy. In the pre-AI era, specifications were often treated as disposable artifacts — necessary for planning but quickly outdated as the real work happened in code. Code was the source of truth. In the AI era, the spec is the source of truth, and code is a generated artifact that derives its quality from the spec.

The “shift left” concept comes from testing, where moving quality checks earlier in the development cycle reduces costs. Applied to AI coding, shift left means moving from “fix bugs in code” to “prevent bugs in specs.” A bug in the spec produces buggy code across every AI agent that reads it. A well-written spec produces correct code on the first attempt.

Shoemaker’s controversial take — “I don’t read code anymore” — sparked significant debate on Hacker News. Critics argue that abdicating code review to AI is irresponsible, especially for production systems. Supporters counter that if the spec is correct and the AI generates code from it, reading the code is redundant — you should be reviewing the spec instead. The debate is far from settled, but it highlights how fundamentally the AI era is changing software development workflows.
